title: Made in Canada: Self-Promotion as a Trust Signal, with Lisa Bragg

host.name: Nola Simon
host.title: Futurist & Founder, Everyday Futurism
host.credentials: 17 years in cross-border insurance operations · Creator of the Assumption-Ground Audit

guest.name: Lisa Bragg
guest.title: Author, speaker and workshop facilitator
guest.credentials: Author of Bragging Rights: How to Talk about Your Work Using Purposeful Self-Promotion · Former TV reporter and anchor · Founded and ran a content company for 16 years

abstract: Lisa Bragg, author of Bragging Rights, makes the case that talking about your work is a trust signal, not a character flaw. Her research, the largest survey on bragging and self-promotion, found people who knew they had lost money and career-defining opportunities because they had been conditioned to stay hidden gems. The conversation covers keeping written records of praise, why what sounds like boasting depends on who is listening, teaching from the scar instead of the wound, amplifying evergreen ideas instead of always making something new, and what TED stages teach about imperfection.
takeaways: Name your wins in writing: when someone praises your work in passing, send a thank-you email that captures what they said, so the record exists at review time.
Run your own record even when nobody else does. If good work goes unremarked, write it down anyway, because no one cares about your future the way you do.
Map the context before you share a success. What reads as normal shop talk to peers can sound like showing off to family or outsiders.
Surface the lessons from hard experiences only once they have healed: teach from the scar, not the wound, and remember that not everyone gets the same latitude to be vulnerable.
Run evergreen ideas again instead of chasing new content: amplify them that day, that week, that year and on their anniversary.

keyQA.question: Why is bragging so uncomfortable?
keyQA.answer: Lisa Bragg wrote Bragging Rights because she kept asking why we are afraid to talk about our successes. In her research, the largest survey on bragging and self-promotion, people told her they knew they had lost millions of dollars or career-defining opportunities because they had been conditioned to stay hidden gems.

keyQA.question: How do you keep a record of praise when it is only given verbally?
keyQA.answer: Thank the person in writing. Nola Simon describes a director who stopped putting compliments in writing, so Nola emailed her afterwards to say thank you for stopping by and here is what you said, then uploaded that to her review file. Lisa adds that if no one praises good work, you should write it down anyway.

keyQA.question: What does it mean to teach from the scar, not the wound?
keyQA.answer: Lisa uses Michael Caine's advice to use the difficulty: hard experiences can become what you teach from, but only once they have healed. She also cautions that unless you are at the top of a big company, you have to watch how vulnerable you are, so be authentic and still watch your back.

keyQA.question: What is Lisa Bragg's favourite interview question?
keyQA.answer: When do you wish you were bolder? People often answer with stories they have never told before, such as standing by when they now recognize racism, sexism or ableism, and the growth since then is what makes the answers worth hearing.
